utterances.text: I don't recall if they were. I probably would have noticed had there been that much light. I probably would have noticed. I would have taken note of that, if there were as much light as is represented in this photograph.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now I would like you to look at the newspaper photograph that I showed you a bit earlier. It is there in front of you on your right. If that is Hangar 6, you see the same windows there along the top of that wall that you see in the photograph, do you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot say that this is the photograph from that place, because I cannot recognise anyone there. I cannot recognise it as a photograph. It could be a copy or something.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Compare it with photograph number 30. See if it doesn't look like the same building.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It looks to me that in these photographs there is something white, some horizontal ... I don't know what they are. They are ... In this photograph, number 30, I see that this has been painted and looks neat. These windows were not there for sure. Had there been this much light, I would have known. It is certain that there was not this much light.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now you are talking about the windows along the left side? JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: I think we will have to have a break for 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: When we come back, we will know how to tackle this issue. (3.45 pm) (Short break) (4.15 pm) (Witness returns to court) JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Remind him he is on his oath.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I am reminding you, sir, that you are still on your oath?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to have photograph number 30 returned to the ELMO, please. Mr. Kuljanin, I want to again direct your attention to that same photograph, number 30. The windows that appear on the right-hand side of that photograph up in the wall, those are the windows that you told us a moment ago were not there when you were there; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The way they look in this photograph and the way I see it in this photograph, that's not how they were. There was tin there and as far as I can see in these photographs there are openings there or there is even glass there. There is either an opening or it has glass on it. When I was there, down there, it was all tin. Here I see a lot of light, and the whole window seems open. When I was there that part you could never open in this way, and I can't see from here whether there is glass here or there's nothing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when you were there even during the day it was pretty dark inside the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was pretty dark. It wasn't dark. It was not dark. It was -- you could see.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There were no windows through which significant light was coming, however?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember. As I recall, there were no windows through which any major light, major amount of light could pass through.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now I would like you to look at the diagram that is in front of you. Look in front of you at the model, over here. See where I am pointing, the model (pointing)?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Look at the model and look at Hangar 6. On the back of Hangar 6 you will see what appears to be four windows. Do you see what I am talking about (pointing)?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I see on this model that windows have been indicated. There are four of them from the side opposite to where the entrance was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So I understand from your testimony just now that those windows did not exist at the time you were there; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Please, I have given this explanation about five times. The windows as they appear in this photograph were not there. You can see that there are openings there either with the glass or without glass. However, there were openings on this side on which these windows are indicated there, and instead of the glass or the empty openings there was tin. So when it was closed it could be opened a little bit at an angle, a little bit, but you could not see through the window fully.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when it was closed, you could not see through it at all; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct. If it was completely closed you could not see through it at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now could I ask -- sorry, Mr. Usher, you have cleared back over there. Could I ask that the roof of Hangar 6 on the model be removed? I think it is E on the model. Yes. Would you stand up so you can see inside, please. You see no canal in there, do you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not see any canal there. I don't think it has been indicated there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So again it's not accurate based upon your recollection of what Celebici looked like; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The canal did exist and I claim that it did exist because it would be plugged up a number of times, and it would be -- our urine would be there and it stank. So we cleaned it several times, as often as we were allowed to. As I say, the canal was 30 cms long. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: It was not accurate, this model; that is what he asked, in view of what you knew?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't see the canal there, and the canal did exist, so it's not the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. That is all I was trying to find out.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Again, if I can assist the Trial Chamber, this model was prepared in 1996. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: I think we appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, your Honours, it may well then be appropriate that this model then be removed from the court room, since it is not representative of 1992, which is the time we are talking about here. If it is a 1996 model and everybody is going to say it is inaccurate, then I think we should get it out of here and get one in here that represents what happened in 1992, because we are not talking about Celebici in 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, along that vein, I have prepared a written motion to strike Prosecutor's exhibits number 1 and 2. I have an original to be filed with the Trial Chamber and a copy for the Prosecutor. I was unable to make nine copies on the break. It is based on Mr. Ostberg's statement that these models are based on 1996 and we don't know whether it fully, fairly and accurately depicts what it purports to depict, that is the camp in 1992. In fact, we have testimony here today from a prosecution witness that it doesn't fully, fairly and accurately depict what it purports to depict. Therefore, your Honours, it is flat not relevant. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: I appreciate your argument. It depends on whether it represents what they are making it to represent. The fact that it is of a later date by itself does not really mean it might not represent certain things for the proposals which they are making.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I agree, your Honour. If the prosecution wants to represent for the record that it is only intended to represent the camp conditions in 1996, then that is another thing. If the Prosecution is suggesting that this represents the way the camp looked in 1992, then I think it should not be here, because it is not accurate. If they want to represent that it is a 1996 representation of the camp, then with that being part of the record, I would have no objection. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: I see your point. I think it depends.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Well, it gives a general layout of the plan, nothing more than that, if you want to say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's even acceptable, Judge Jan. Thank you. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: It is almost impossible to reconstruct the 1992 conditions. I do not know who could have done it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We will have some videotapes that were made in 1992 that will give the court a little bit better idea of what it looked like, I am sure. Okay. May I proceed? JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Yes, you can.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Mr. Kuljanin, you talked about a time that journalists came to the camp; correct? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't know exactly what agency those journalists were from, do you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us as nearly as you can the date upon which the journalists came to the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot give the exact date when they came.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is your best estimate of the date that they came?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot recall. I know that they had cameras with them and that they were shooting. Delic was there with them and they spoke something. I did not understand the language and what they were talking about, but they were shooting some footage, and Delic would put his foot on someone's chest. They made loud comments --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Objection, your Honour. This is non-responsive. The question was: "What is your best estimate ..." -- JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: He is being asked to see whether he can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The question is: does he know when it was. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Whether circumstances make you remember a particular date.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Was it closer to the time you got there or closer to the time you left there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was somewhere in the middle, maybe around the middle somewhere. It wasn't close to the end and it was not close to the beginning, so somewhere in the middle, maybe early August or late July, somewhere around there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it before or after the Red Cross came?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot recall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the front gate simply left open during the day so that journalists could come any time they wanted to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They didn't stay long. They came that day, those journalists. I think they must have come from a foreign country. I couldn't understand the language, and the local journalists with cameras would come -- they would come too but I don't know when. I don't know when that was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So journalists were coming to the camp not infrequently. Occasionally journalists would come to the camp; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said twice. You say frequently. If twice is frequently, I don't know. I said twice. Once they were foreigners. I couldn't understand the language they spoke and the second time I think they must have been from the local Konjic television station. A man came with a camera. He shot all of us and at that moment he said: "I have no more tape", and he left. So I don't think that is often.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So those pictures that were taken by the journalists on the two occasions that they came there should show the prisoners in an emaciated condition, near starvation with bruises all over their bodies from the starvation and the beatings, should they not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot remember exactly what we looked like at that minute, because I have no orientation to go by. Just before the International Red Cross came and after they left they reduced the beatings, and they always said: "Don't beat people in the face." I heard Delic say that and Zenga too. "Don't beat them in the face, on the head." So we could conclude from that that something was about to happen. After some time the International Red Cross came. After their first visit -- they stayed a whole day and they left. Three minutes after they left, they barged in. They beat us up, but again not our heads. The next day the International Red Cross came back. They were a little surprised, I think. People showed their bruises on their body, not on their head. They didn't hit anyone on the head. So this means that this was intentional. So, therefore, on these shots this will probably not be seen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You talked about several people who -- in fact, you made a list of people who you claim died at Celebici and you went through that list. You didn't conclude in the course of any of that testimony that any of those persons died of starvation, from lack of food, did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Together, hunger and the torture, all kinds of torture we were exposed to, psychological and physical mistreatment, coupled with the shortage of food, and the lack of medicines and treatment, together with the beatings up -- all these things together contributed to people dying or being killed, and so on. I think when you take all that together people did die and they suffered terribly. It is possible that if they had had more food -- I don't know. I can't guarantee that they would survive, but maybe they would have had a chance, a greater chance, or if they hadn't been beaten more people would have survived.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of course, if there had not been a war, more people would have survived; correct? Yes? (Pause.) Many people were killed in the war one way or another, were they not, and died in the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Of course. The answer is self-evident. If there had not been any war, people would not get killed. Of course, people normally get killed in a war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us the first day that you recall seeing Mr. Landzo, Zenga, at Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember the exact date, but maybe after some ten days or so, ten days or so after my arrival, that I noticed it. He may have been there, but I didn't notice him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. What is the last day that you remember seeing Esad Landzo, Zenga, at Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember when he left, but I know that he left to -- the military police, to join the military police, and I know that because I saw him leaving, and when he was promoted to the military police he would come occasionally. It was almost impossible to get under the fence. He would take off his tee-shirt and he would be wearing only trousers. He would creep under the wire fence and come to the hangar to ask money from Dusko Bendjo, for instance. Then he would disappear again, but I don't remember when that was. Maybe -- he left Celebici, I think, before I was transferred to Musala perhaps, maybe some 20 days before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He was not there when the Red Cross came, was he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot recall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He was not there -- certainly not there the full time that you were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean until 31st August, for as long as I was there?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He wasn't there all the time. I don't know when he left, on what date but he wasn't there throughout my stay there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So some of the torture activity at least you have described to this court he simply could not have been involved in because he was not there; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know what period you are referring to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The whole period. You described almost daily beatings through the whole 95 days or so that you were there. For several of those days at least Mr. Landzo could not have been involved, because he was not there. That is all I am asking. I think it is simple.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is a very complicated question, because he would come occasionally in a uniform and they were saying that Landzo had joined the police. So he would show off a little being a policeman. So when he was transferred, or rather promoted, to the police, he would come and visit. He would go somewhere there, I don't know where, whether it was within the compound or outside, but he would pass by, and he would go to the swimming pool to bathe. We would see him going along the railway line and then coming back again. Occasionally he would enter the hangar and -- not as much as before while he was there permanently -- he didn't beat people as much and torture them as much -- but he would come by, beat a couple of people and then go off again. This would happen occasionally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So he kind of stopped by on his way to the swimming pool just to engage in a couple of beatings just for fun; is that what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's exactly what I am saying.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is the same person you just told us a few moments ago that when it got real hot inside the building he would spray water inside the building so it would be cooler for the prisoners. Is that the same person you are talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We are talking about the same person. Not to cool it off. They wouldn't give us water to swallow. People were almost fainting from thirst. He was spraying the water, whereas we were dry. They would not let us have a drop of water. He would come in and say: "Are you thirsty, you Cetniks?" He would curse our mothers. He would laugh and beat somebody. Then he would go out again. This would go on sometimes for two or three hours. He would not give us a drop of water while doing that. That is why he was doing that and not to cool off the building. He did it also when it was too cool.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I did not ask you a question, did I?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have not completed my answer. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: I think you have.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think you have.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I haven't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now you were closed up in this Building Number 6. You were forced to sit there with your head down between your knees. If you raised your head, you were beaten unmercifully, and yet you would see Landzo walking along the railway tracks, going to the swimming pool, climbing in under the fence, and so I guess what you have described as your total confinement in that building with your head between your legs is untrue. You had a great deal of freedom to walk around outside and see what was going on out there. Is that the case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I claim with full responsibility that that is not correct, the way you have put it. If you allow me, I can tell you what it was like in five or six sentences. The discipline improved a little when Landzo left and after the visit of the International Red Cross. They would let us go to the toilet, for instance. They would take people to do labour. Some people were digging something. Some were loading and unloading. Some were cleaning. At those times all of us could see something. We weren't blindfolded so we would go here and there. Someone would see this, someone else something else. So when you are told to go and dig, of course you can cast a glance left and right. There were guards who were correct, who would say: "Sit down and have a smoke, have a cigarette." There were such cases too. For instance, once when I was loading those trucks, the man offered us cigarettes and he said to us: "Boys, take a break and have a cigarette." Then we exchanged a few words. There were such moments maybe in Number 6 too, but these were very rare occasions. I can't say this happened on 21st or 22nd at 3 o'clock or at 10 o'clock. There were such cases. Delic too would come. He would hit a man. The man fell. He would lift him up, give him a cigarette and then that man would have to smoke. There were such cases and, of course, you saw these things. They didn't blindfold us so that we couldn't see anything. There were cases when a guard who came from Bijela -- I don't remember his name; I don't know his name -- he would piggy-back -- ride piggy-back and sometimes we could see this. So we had to go out sometimes to eat. We were given one or two spoonfuls of something, sometimes three, sometimes four. As you take a spoon to your mouth, of course you will see what's happening around up. So there were such situations. Or when you go to the toilet, until you reach the toilet, you see things. People were taken for interrogation to the command building. Some people once, other people several times, and they saw things. Then they had to dig that bunker near Zenga. I didn't go, and, of course, they couldn't spend all day looking at the ground. Those people had to turn their heads around and see things. There were such moments. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Thank you very much. You explained how relaxed you were later.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: How many times were you taken to the infirmary in Building 22?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't go to the infirmary or Number 22 at all. I asked for help. I asked for it ten times. Nobody reacted and then I said: "If I have to die, let me die."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many times did you go to the infirmary in Building 22?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not once.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it your testimony then that doctors came from there to Building 6 to examine you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The examination consisted of a question: "What's wrong with you? What's wrong with that one?" He had about ten or fifteen minutes. At one point there were 255 of us. As soon as a man answered and said what was wrong, he just shrugged his shoulders and went on to the next man. He would say: "I cannot help you." He would tour the building and that was it. But I am not saying that some people didn't go to the infirmary, especially before the International Red Cross came, so that they wouldn't see so much. They tried to patch up the injuries, to cover up the situation. Prior to the arrival of the International Red Cross they would take people there. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: This is your witness. It is most unusual for counsel to sit down when his witness is testifying.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if the witness wants to simply make speeches, then I do not want to get in his way. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Then you will provoke such speeches and they will be made.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I cannot imagine that asking him if a doctor came to see him in Hangar 6 would provoke a speech like that. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: He is telling us what happened when the doctor came.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But I never asked him that question. I just asked him if a doctor came. What he did was launch into another one of his speeches. I think he has come here to make speeches. Maybe it would be appropriate to allow him to make speeches. If the court allows, I will go ahead and finish. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: It is a witness for the prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. I think I have no further questions to ask you, Mr. Kuljanin. Thank you. Oh, I do have one more. What was the name of the doctor that came to the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't give you have a direct answer. It wasn't one doctor. There were two doctors, Relja Mrkajic and Petko Grubac. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: The doctor that came to examine you. That is all he wants.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Who was the doctor that you talked to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I asked assistance from Relja Mrkajic. He shrugged his shoulders and said: "There's nothing I can do for you."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Relja Mrkajic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Relja Mrkajic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is a doctor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He is a specialist.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. That is all I have. Thank you. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: I suppose that is the end of the defence cross-examination. Any re-examination on the part of the prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, your Honour. Two issues only. Re-examination by MR. OSTBERG.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: I will ask some questions that have come forward through the cross-examination. I will not ask you a "yes" or "no" question, but I will ask you to wait to answer it until I have finished my question. When I examined you and asked you what kind of methods Esad Landzo used when he mistreated you, you mentioned several things, but you never mentioned a knife. In cross-examination you said that you have been hit by him by a knife. Will you expand on that event, please? Will you tell us more about what happened then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can in detail, because I remember it well. On that occasion Zenga had a semi-automatic rifle with a knife attached. He came up to me and asked me: "How are you?" I said -- what else could I say but: "Okay." At that moment he suddenly hit me with this knife here (indicating), but I managed to move away, so he tore my shirt only. A second time he pricked me in the forehead. So I immediately vomited something green -- I apologise -- and then I felt -- I couldn't see properly for a moment. Then he became really mad and then he pierced between people's heads -- he pierced the walls with this bayonet. Why he asked me how I was and all that I don't know. There was absolutely no reason. He simply came up to me. It occurred to him to ask this question and that's what happened. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: This is now sufficient for the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: I am quite satisfied with this account of what happened with the knife. I have one other issue. When learned counsel for Mucic examined you and tried to force you to answer "yes" or "no", you entered a discussion --

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am bound to say that I do not care for the characterisation "force". I wonder whether my learned friend would like to reconsider that word and withdraw it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Tried to make him answer every question "yes" or "no". You entered a discussion on Mucic's position in the camp. Before counsel finished his questioning you said that you had other facts to found your answer on than your visits -- his visits to the Hangar 6. I will ask: what other facts would you found your answer on Mucic's position on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The facts are that all women who thought they were helping their husband or brothers went to Pavo Mucic --

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I would just like to stop the witness, please, so I can address you on a matter of law, please. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: This is completely irrelevant. He could not be giving any opinion of this nature. It is an opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: I asked the question on what facts he based it. The facts I got so far we cannot accept, of course. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Which are those facts? The facts outside?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: The facts outside the visits of Mucic to the hangar. That was my question. On which facts he based his statement that Mucic was the camp commander. That is what I was looking for. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Do you not think this is irrelevant in terms of what he wants to say because he was not in a position to see those things?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: As he just said. I asked him if he had any facts which he could bring to the court on which he based this statement. If he has not got any, I have no further questions, of course. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: He has none, because these are all speculations.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: What we heard so far was speculation. Thank you. Then we have no further questions. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: This is all you have for the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: That is all I have for the witness. Thank you. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Thank you very much for your efforts and your patience I would say. Thank you very much for your contribution. So you are discharged.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours. I apologise if sometimes I was a little nervous. I hope you will have understanding for my position then and today too, and this is the first time for me to address a court of law. I was also reminded of the camp and this is very painful for me. So I really do apologise if I made any mistakes. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you too. (Witness withdrew) JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Who is your next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Your Honour, our next witness was supposed to be protected from media and public, but he decided not to be protected any more. So I call Mr. Mladen Kuljanin as our next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: How many Kuljanins are there in this case?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Many, your Honour. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Swear him. Swear the witness. MR. MLADEN KULJANIN (sworn) Examined by MR. TURONE JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: You can take your seat. Sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (In interpretation): thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: May I proceed, your Honour? JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Yes, you can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, would you please state your full name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mladen Kuljanin, born in Konjic 15th June 1971. I lived in the village of Bradina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is your ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Serbian.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you born in Bradina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, in Konjic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kuljanin, what education did you receive? I mean, what kind of schools did you attend for many years?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 11 years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which kind of schools?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Restaurant school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your profession in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Baker.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is Bradina where you lived at the beginning of May 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, was there a time when Bradina was affected by the armed conflict in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. On 25th May 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a time on which you were arrested?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 27th May 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that -- approximately at what time that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Around 11 o'clock in the morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Can you briefly explain the circumstances of your arrest?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 27th May 1992 I was at home with my father, mother and my sister. We came out around 11.30, my father, my sister and my mother. We stepped outside and across our house, in front of the restaurant of Mica Kuljanin there were already a number of detained persons and we joined them. When I arrived there there were soldiers of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and soldiers of the HVO who were present there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mean you were arrested by these persons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there insignia on their uniforms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. There were lilies of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and there was the chequerboard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that -- you said in front of a restaurant?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which restaurant was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was the restaurant called Mico in Bradina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, how many soldiers were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I arrived in front of the cafe there were about 60 soldiers. I cannot recollect the exact number.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who were the commanders of these soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not recognise -- I did not know who the commander was there in front of the cafe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know personally some of these people, some of these soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Well, your Honour, he has just answered the question: "I did not recognise anybody." That I think is the answer: "I did not know anybody."

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: He was answering about the commanders. I was asking about any one of these 60 soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: He said: "Did you personally know some of these people?" It seems to me that refers to the question that has already been asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: My previous question was about the commanders. Now my question is about the possibility he might have known anybody among the general number of the soldiers. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Frankly I do not know what is a commander and who were the soldiers. If you were referring to the command structure, who were the commanders, if he did not know that, that is quite different from ordinary soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Exactly. My next question was whether he knows any of the soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: With -- JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: When you use the word "commander", it is --

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: With respect, I invite your Honour to say there is no relevance in the question of who the soldiers were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: How is it important who were the soldiers? He was arrested.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Kuljanin, were you told why you were being arrested?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any weapon at the time of your arrest?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you a member of any armed group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you in any way take part in the defence of the village of Bradina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you approximately say, if you know, how many persons in your village were armed at the outbreak of the conflict?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot say. In fact, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, Mr. Kuljanin, what happened to you after you were arrested?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I was arrested in front of the restaurant Mico and I was -- and members of the HVO and the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina were passing around a photograph, but none of us was able to recognise this photograph, and so at the very start there we were being beaten. After about one hour in front of the Mico restaurant where we were lined up we were taken to the centre of Bradina. We walked on foot about 2 kms. When I arrived in the centre of Bradina, we were made to lean against a wall. It was about 10 metres long. We stood there about an hour and a half with our hands up. For one hour we were being beaten there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many of you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time we were 60-70.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By whom were you beaten?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and members of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With what were you beaten?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Rifle butts. They kicked us. With sticks, hands and other objects, whatever they had at hand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After that we were loaded into a vehicle of Fap make. It had a canopy. There were 60 of us and one by one we jumped onto this vehicle. As we were jumping in everybody was being beaten. As I was coming in somebody -- one of the soldiers hit me and I fell down to the road. I fell unconscious. When I tried -- when I came to and tried a second time he hit me again, but I was able to climb onto this vehicle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. What happened then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When all 60 of us were on the vehicle, they took us to the Celebici camp and we arrived there around 1 o'clock. There we were -- there were other people who were waiting for us in the camouflage uniforms. When the vehicle came to the gate of the Celebici camp we had to jump off and line up against a wall again. We were against this wall for about five hours, somewhere between 1.00 and 7.00. As we were lined up against the wall they ordered us to strip to the waist and to take off our socks. Then they ordered -- there were two or three groups that were taking shifts in beating us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where exactly inside the camp did this act happen?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Your Honour, that is a leading question. The witness has not yet said where exactly, whether it was inside or outside the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: He said he arrived at Celebici.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: He said: "We came to the gate." It does not say whether he was inside or outside the camp. Counsel must not lead his witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: All right. Could you say exactly where did this beating happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Inside the Celebici camp. We entered the Celebici camp. We passed the gate and we entered inside.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. In which point of the camp inside the camp did that happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Against the wall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kuljanin, you see a model in front of you. Can you recognise this model?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It represents the Celebici camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I may ask the usher to provide something to point to the witness. So could you please stand up and point out the position of this wall inside the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please do it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Pointing).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For the record, the witness pointed at the wall near the entrance of the camp. Maybe you say that already. How long did you remain approximately at that wall? How long did this beating last?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From 1.00 in the afternoon until about 7.00 at night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the people hitting you say anything during the beating?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember something you heard?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were saying: "Auschwitz. This is Islam. Jamahera! Long live Islam! Allah! Allah is the greatest!"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How were you personally beaten? With what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was kicked. Then I was beaten with a rifle butt and with different objects. There were chains and there were sticks, and there were some cables for electricity. I don't know how thick they were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you indicate the name of any of the persons taking part in this beating?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I recognised two persons at that time. There was Hazim Delic and Mario Matic. Mario Matic went together with me to school in Sarajevo. I recognised him. He was one of the first who came over to me and hit me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know Hazim Delic from before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From sight.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you get to know his name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were people there who worked together with him in the Sip Prenj company and they recognised him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe the physical consequences you suffered from this particular beating at the wall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On site Petko Gligorevic was killed and Gojko Miljenic died from the injuries.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am sorry, Mr. Kuljanin. My question is about the physical consequences that you suffered personally from this particular beating, you suffered?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My consequences? After that beating I could not urinate. I had to squat in order to urinate. I couldn't urinate standing. They beat me mostly in the kidney area and then at the back, but they did not choose much where they were beating. Every part of my body had suffered blows.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you receive any medical care after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anybody inside the camp enquire about this incident?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you now describe the physical consequences which any other person, any other prisoner suffered after this particular beating at the wall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. About 10 metres away from me was Petko Gligorevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Petko?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Petko Gligorevic. He was about 10 metres away from me. At one point he fell down from beating and some soldiers came over and ordered two prisoners to pull him up. Then he got up. When the next group came over to beat us, Petko fell down again and never got up again. He remained there dead. Gojko Miljenic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you personally see about Miljanic Gojko?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Gojko Miljenic was beaten up but arrived alive to Hangar Number 6 and the next morning he was dead. I personally was with Gojko when we arrived in the hangar, when we were locked up there. Blood was coming out of Gojko's ears and his chest was all broken. He could not talk. He just gurgled and blood was coming out of his mouth and his ears and the next day when the dawn came Gojko was dead from having been beaten. Miroslav Vujicic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you see about him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When they started beating us Miroslav Vujicic tried to run, because I guess he would try to escape, because they were beating us. A shot was fired. He fell. A soldier came forward and there was -- he was a metre away from him and the second shot rang out and Miroslav was dead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is there any other detail you personally eyewitnessed in these hours of beating?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Dragan Kravar. I personally brought him to the hangar in a wheelbarrow, because he could not go on his own power. He could not walk from having been beaten.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kuljanin, what happened to you after this beating, after this long beating at the wall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then we were moved to Hangar Number 6, where I spent 180 days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe the physical characteristics of building 6?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please do that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The length was maybe 12, 13 metres. I don't know exactly. I could not really concentrate much in those moments. The width was 5 or 6 metres. There were several windows, one entrance door that we came in and out from.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did every prisoner have a given position inside Hangar 6?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you say how were the prisoners distributed inside Hangar 6? I mean, how were the positions organised inside the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were two rows in the middle where the prisoners sat and there were two rows around.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you personally maintain the same position during the whole period inside Hangar 6?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I moved twice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May I ask that the witness be provided with a photograph of Prosecution Exhibit number 1, page 7 and can it be placed on the ELMO so that the witness might show us the different positions he had inside the hangar?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Did he not prepare a plan for you like the other witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Did he not prepare a plan for you, like the other witnesses have done?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: He did never prepare a plan. Do you recognise this plan as a map of Hangar 6, Mr. Kuljanin? Can you indicate the door on the hangar, pointing with a pencil to the map itself? I cannot see on the ELMO this map. Can you point the door?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Pointing).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you now indicate on this map your three positions -- the first position, first of all, you had inside Number 6?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Pointing) Here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please mark a cross on that point and mark it with a number "1" so that we might understand that this is the first position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Marking).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please now indicate to us the second position you had inside the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Marking).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Number 2, okay. Then the third position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Marking).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much. Was there any particular reason for which you changed position twice inside Hangar 6?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know the reason. Some people were released, that is transferred to Musala, to the sports hall. Then as they were moved there we were moved.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that your initiative or somebody had you moved to another position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was not my choice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you say very approximately when did you move from position 1 to position 2?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some time in July, in July.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mean you moved from the first to the second position in July?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, July, August.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you say again approximately when did you move from position number 2 to position number 3?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: September, October, thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Your Honours, if there are no objection, I would like to tender this map as a prosecution exhibit, since it marks exactly the three different positions, and it will be Exhibit Number 28 -- 98, I beg your pardon, if it is admitted. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Have you shown it to the defence? Show it to the defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I have no objection to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, subject to the reliability of the map itself, which I think we will discuss at a later point when I file my motion, I have no objection to it. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: It is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. By the way, do you remember anything particular about the floor of Hangar Number 6? How was the floor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was concrete.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember any detail besides that or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kuljanin, how were the conditions of life in Number 6, in Hangar Number 6, drinking water, food, toilet, etc? Let us start with drinking water. How were the drinking water supplies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were getting drinking water in bottles, not as much as we wanted but as much as they were giving us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you receive drinking water every day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not every single day. Sometimes it would be every third day that we would get water and food.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about food? How was the food supply?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was terrible and the food was bad. I can say it was below any standard and insufficient. We were receiving one bread of 600, 700 grams, divided between fifteen people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you receive food every day anyway?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not every day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the period of time which you might remain -- might have remained without food? How long?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The longest period that we did not receive any food was three days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the toilet facilities? How were the toilet facilities when you were in Hangar 6?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The toilet was made by the prisoners outside. They dug it up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you permitted to go outside for toilet facilities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Sometimes, not always.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How was that organised?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For a period of time it would be 20 people going out to pee and we had about 20 seconds to do it, the 20 of us, and the International Red Cross was present there, and once, on one occasion, Hazim Delic took us out, and a representative of the Red Cross was present and he watched, and it was 90 seconds for 20 people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the sleeping facilities? Did you have blankets and other things like that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I slept on concrete for three months. For a period of time we couldn't even sleep. We had to sit up day and night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Uh-huh. Sir, approximately how many prisoners did you observe being inside Hangar 6 when you first arrived in the hangar? JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Mr. Turone, we will have to break here and continue in the afternoon tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: All right, your Honour. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: So the Trial Chamber will rise and we will reassemble at 2.30 tomorrow. 2.30. Please. (5.35 pm)
